claim: The hologenome concept proposes that microbes and their host organism are an independent unit of selection.
source: The hologenome concept proposes that microbes and their host organism are an independent unit of selection.
evidence: This is a statement about the hologenome concept presented in the abstract, supported by the theoretical framework of the study.

claim: The microbiomes of cold-resistant fish showed higher resilience to temperature changes.
source: The microbiomes of cold-resistant fish showed higher resilience to temperature changes, indicating that the microbiome is shaped by its host's selection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing microbiome responses in resistant vs. sensitive fish groups.

claim: The gut microbiome facilitates key adaptations during cold exposure by promoting energy demand-driven regulation in mice.
source: Recent work in mice revealed that the gut microbiome facilitates key adaptations during cold exposure by promoting energy demand-driven regulation (Chevalier et al., 2015; Rosenberg and Zilber-Rosenberg, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on mice.

claim: Gut microbial communities are vital for host survival, homeostasis, development and functioning.
source: many studies have already proven the vital importance of gut microbial communities for host survival, homeostasis, development and functioning (McFall-Ngai et al., 2013; Shabat et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Poikilothermic organisms must develop strategies to maintain homeostasis within diverse temperature gradients.
source: Poikilothermic organisms, such as fish, must develop strategies to maintain homeostasis within diverse temperature gradients because environmental temperature changes would otherwise disrupt homeostasis and cause deleterious effects on vital physiological functions (Guschina and Harwood, 2006; Vinagre et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and represents established knowledge about poikilothermic organisms.

claim: Temperature affects microbial communities in aquatic environments as a habitat-filtering force.
source: Microbial communities in aquatic environments have also been reported to be affected by abiotic factors that act as a habitat-filtering force, such as temperature (Fuhrman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The growth of tilapia species is highly affected by temperature and they are subject to growth inhibition and mortality when exposed to low temperatures.
source: The growth of these fish species is highly affected by temperature; they are subject to growth inhibition and mortality when exposed to low temperatures (Cnaani et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on tilapia.

claim: Recent work revealed transgenerational inheritance of cold tolerance in tilapia species.
source: However, recent work revealed transgenerational inheritance of cold tolerance in these species (Nitzan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Temperature was the major factor shaping microbial community diversity and richness within the fish gut.
source: Linear mixed-effects model analysis indicated that temperature was the major factor shaping microbial community diversity and richness within the fish gut (Table 1; FShannon = 46.43, FRichness = 45.79, p = 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Table 1.

claim: There was a dramatic decrease in microbial diversity when both groups were exposed to cold temperature.
source: Indeed, we found a dramatic decrease (Figure 2Ai; Wilcoxon t-test, two-sided, 95% confidence interval (CI), p = 7.2E-02) in microbial diversity (Shannon index H')
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and visualization in Figure 2Ai.

claim: There was a dramatic decrease in microbial richness when both groups were exposed to cold temperature.
source: and richness (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Wilcoxon t-test, two-sided, 95% CI, p = 2.7E-08; Figure 2—figure supplement 2, rarefaction curves) when both groups were exposed to cold temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and visualization in supplementary figures.

claim: The decrease in microbial diversity was in agreement with the low-temperature decrease in the 16S gene copy numbers.
source: This decrease was in agreement with the low-temperature decrease in the 16S gene copy numbers (real-time PCR; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Low-temperature conditions are very selective and potentially constrain microbial communities, decreasing their inter-individual variation.
source: suggesting that low-temperature conditions are very selective and potentially constrain microbial communities, decreasing their inter-individual variation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed data on richness variability.

claim: Microbial community structure (β-diversity) was dramatically affected by cold exposure.
source: Microbial community structure (β-diversity) was also dramatically affected by cold exposure, being the major factor associated with increasing similarity between individuals in the communities (Table 2; FTemperature = 6.5072, p = 0.002), after gut physiology effects (FPart = 28.8936, p = 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis presented in Table 2.

claim: Orders from the Proteobacteria phylum, specifically Vibrionales and Alteromonadales, were enriched at 12°C.
source: Orders from the Proteobacteria phylum, and more specifically Vibrionales and Alteromonadales, were enriched at 12°C (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1, Table S1; Figure 2—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures and supplementary tables.

claim: Vibrionales and Alteromonadales taxa have potential for survival in cold temperatures according to prior studies.
source: with prior studies reporting these taxa's potential for survival in cold temperatures (Lauro et al., 2011; Math et al., 2012; Raymond-Bouchard and Whyte, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Several microbial phyla, such as Planctomycetes, Bacteroidetes and Verrucomicrobia, were significantly depleted after cold-exposure.
source: several microbial phyla, such as Planctomycetes, Bacteroidetes and Verrucomicrobia, were significantly depleted after cold-exposure (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 5; Supplementary file 1, Table S1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures and supplementary tables.

claim: In poikilothermic vertebrates such as the blue tilapia, gut microbial communities are strongly affected by environmental temperature.
source: These findings indicate that in poikilothermic vertebrates such as the blue tilapia, gut microbial communities are strongly affected by environmental temperature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Host thermal tolerance has a significant effect on gut microbial diversity.
source: We compared the gut microbial compositions of the sensitive and resistant families and found that host thermal tolerance has a significant effect on gut microbial diversity (Table 2; FTolerance = 2.2269, p = 0.04).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis presented in Table 2.

claim: There is a significant interaction between host thermal tolerance and temperature on microbiome response.
source: Furthermore, we also observed a significant interaction between host thermal tolerance and temperature, indicating a different microbiome response to the lower temperature in the resistant vs. sensitive hosts (FTxT = 3.6113, p = 0.012).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the interaction effect.

claim: When fish from both groups were kept under optimal temperature conditions of 24°C, the sensitive fish exhibited higher microbial diversity than the resistant ones.
source: Interestingly, when fish from both groups were kept under their optimal temperature conditions of 24°C, the sensitive fish exhibited higher microbial diversity (Shannon H′) than the resistant ones, as well as higher individual variability (Figure 2Aii; Wilcoxon t-test, two-sided, 95% CI, p = 0.048).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and visualization in Figure 2Aii.

claim: Cold-resistant fish had a higher within-group microbiome similarity than the sensitive fish under optimal conditions.
source: Indeed, when we compared the β-diversity of the two groups under these optimal conditions, we found that cold-resistant fish had a higher within-group microbiome similarity than the sensitive fish (Figure 2Ci; non-parametric Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.01, using 1000 Monte Carlo permutations)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and visualization in Figure 2Ci.

claim: Host genetic background (genetic selection for cold tolerance) had a strong effect on shaping the microbiome composition.
source: We found that the individuals from both high- and low-diversity microbiomes (Principal coordinate analysis; Figure 2—figure supplement 6) clustered significantly according to host group (Permanova analysis; Supplementary file 1, Tables S3 and S4), suggesting that host genetic background (genetic selection for cold tolerance) had a strong effect on shaping the microbiome composition.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and visualization in supplementary figures.

claim: Cetobacterium somerae and species of the order Vibrionales were enriched in the resistant fish gut.
source: Taxa including microbial species such as Cetobacterium somerae (Tsuchiya et al., 2008) and species of the order Vibrionales (i.e., Vibrio cholerae; Figure 2—figure supplement 5F), which were also described as microbes surviving in environments with a broad temperature range (Raymond-Bouchard and Whyte, 2017; Townsley et al., 2016), were enriched in the resistant fish gut (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 8; Supplementary file 1, Tables S5 and S6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures and supplementary tables, along with citations to prior research.

claim: A higher diversity of taxa, including Prevotella sp., Streptococcus luteciae and Bacteroidetes species, was enriched in the sensitive fish gut.
source: On the other hand, a higher diversity of taxa, including Prevotella sp., Streptococcus luteciae and Bacteroidetes species, as well as species from the families Christensenellaceae, Succinivibrionaceae and Clostridiaceae,was enriched in the sensitive fish gut (Figure 2D; Supplementary file 1, Tables S5 and S6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures and supplementary tables.

claim: Host genetic background shapes microbiome composition by selecting for specific microbes.
source: Altogether, our results indicate that host genetic background shapes microbiome composition by selecting for specific microbes, with some of them potentially carrying fitness traits for low-temperature tolerance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: After exposure to stressful low-temperature conditions, the microbiomes of cold-resistant fish families were less affected than those of sensitive ones.
source: When we compared the β-diversity within each of these host groups in relation to changing temperature, however, we found that after exposure to the stressful low-temperature conditions, the microbiomes of cold-resistant fish families were less affected than those of sensitive ones (Figure 2Cii; non-parametric Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.02, using 1000 Monte Carlo permutations).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and visualization in Figure 2Cii.

claim: The fold change in the relative abundance of the core microbiome in resistant fish was significantly lower than that in sensitive ones.
source: Similar to the overall microbiome response (Figure 2Cii), the fold change in the relative abundance of the core microbiome in resistant fish was significantly lower than that in sensitive ones (Figure 2Eii).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2Eii.

claim: Quantitative PCR results showed a significantly less pronounced temperature effect on the abundance of the core microbes in the gut of the resistant fish compared to that in the gut of the sensitive ones.
source: Our results were in agreement with the sequencing data (Figure 2Ei, ii), showing a significantly less pronounced temperature effect on the abundance of the core microbes in the gut of the resistant fish compared to that in the gut of the sensitive ones (Figure 2Eiii).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative PCR data shown in Figure 2Eiii.

claim: Host thermal tolerance modulates the microbiome's response to temperature changes.
source: These results thus supported our hypothesis that host thermal tolerance modulates the microbiome's response to temperature changes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: During cold exposure, there was a significant change in several pathways in all host microbiomes, resistant and sensitive.
source: During cold exposure, we found a significant change (enrichment or depletion) in several pathways in all host microbiomes, resistant and sensitive.
evidence: This claim is based on pathway analysis of the microbiome data.

claim: A decrease in the abundance of genes belonging to metabolic pathways was observed during cold exposure.
source: More specifically, a decrease in the abundance of genes belonging to metabolic pathways was observed, whereas genes in pathways related to cellular processes and signaling increased significantly in abundance (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Genes in pathways related to cellular processes and signaling increased significantly in abundance during cold exposure.
source: More specifically, a decrease in the abundance of genes belonging to metabolic pathways was observed, whereas genes in pathways related to cellular processes and signaling increased significantly in abundance (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The overall fold change in microbial coding capacity between warm and cold temperature was significantly greater in the cold-sensitive fish.
source: In line with the changes in microbial composition, the overall fold change in microbial coding capacity between warm and cold temperature was significantly greater in the cold-sensitive fish (Figure 3B; p < 0.0001, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, two-sided)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and visualization in Figure 3B.

claim: Microbiome composition changes resulting from cold exposure relate to functional shifts corresponding to a stress-related response and to cell defense.
source: Specifically, microbiome composition changes resulting from cold exposure seem to relate to functional shifts, which overall correspond to a stress-related response and to cell defense, in line with prior studies suggesting reduction of metabolic activity and transcription, and increases in motility, chemotaxis and membrane transport in response to cold (Nachin et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional analysis of the data and citations to prior research.

claim: Not only microbiome composition, but also certain attributes of the microbiome may be influenced by host genetic background and response to low temperatures.
source: Therefore, host thermal tolerance seems to contribute to and to enhance the differences in microbiome functions with respect to thermal stress, potentially suggesting that not only microbiome composition, but also certain attributes of the microbiome may be influenced by host genetic background and response to low temperatures.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional analysis data.

claim: The overall fold change in gene expression between warm and cold temperature conditions was significantly higher in the cold-sensitive fish.
source: In agreement with our findings of a differential microbiome response to cold exposure between the resistant and sensitive fish, the transcriptomic response in the liver showed that the overall fold change in gene expression between warm and cold temperature conditions was significantly higher in the cold-sensitive fish (Figure 4A; p < 0.0001, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, one-sided)
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptomic analysis and visualization in Figure 4A.

claim: The similarity in the transcript presence/absence patterns of the host response between fish in 24°C and 12°C conditions was significantly higher in the resistant families than in the sensitive ones.
source: Moreover, when we compared the similarity in the transcript presence/absence patterns of the host response between fish in 24°C and 12°C conditions, we found it to be significantly higher in the resistant families than in the sensitive ones, showing a stronger effect of temperature change in the sensitive fish (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptomic analysis and visualization in Figure 4B.

claim: More than 80% of the variance observed in the microbiome response to temperature could be explained by the variance observed in the transcriptomic response.
source: This analysis showed that more than 80% of the variance observed in the microbiome response to temperature could be explained by the variance observed in the transcriptomic response (Figure 4B; actual variance was 83% vs. permuted 44%)
evidence: This claim is supported by Canonical Correlation Analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The measured correlation coefficient between microbiome and transcriptome was significant when compared to correlation coefficients achieved after randomly shuffling the sample labels.
source: Interestingly, the measured correlation coefficient was significant when we compared it to correlation coefficients achieved after randomly shuffling the sample labels (Figure 4B; p = 0.0044).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Several metabolic pathways were affected in both the host transcriptome and the microbiome in response to cold exposure.
source: Notably, when we looked at the host transcriptome response to cold exposure, we found several metabolic pathways (Figure 3C) that were also affected in the microbiome (Figure 3A), with most of the changes occurring in the same direction (depletion or enrichment).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of pathway analysis data shown in Figures 3A and 3C.

claim: Transcription- and cytochrome P450-related pathways were reported as key cell metabolism cold-induced adaptations in homeotherms.
source: Looking at the functions that are commonly shared between the host and the microbiome response to cold exposure (Figure 3C), we found that some of these functions, namely transcription- and cytochrome P450-related pathways (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), were also reported as key cell metabolism cold-induced adaptations in homeotherms (Shore et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the data with citations to prior research.

claim: These functions may be conserved with regard to host and gut microbiome responses to temperature changes.
source: Such findings led us hypothesize that these functions may be conserved with regard to host and gut microbiome responses to temperature changes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed data and comparison with prior research.

claim: Cold exposure led to dramatic changes in gut microbiome composition.
source: Cold exposure led to dramatic changes in gut microbiome composition, representing a notable determinant of the microbial communities, by increasing several orders of Proteobacteria (Vibrionales and Alteromonadales) and decreasing all other phyla (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 2.

claim: Some species of the order Alteromonadales have been shown to facilitate adaptations for survival under different conditions, including low temperatures.
source: In particular, some species of the order Alteromonadales have been shown to facilitate adaptations for survival under different conditions, including low temperatures (Alteromonas [Math et al., 2012]; Shewanella [Abboud et al., 2005])
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Several Vibrionales species have been found to adapt to low temperatures, such as Vibrio cholerae.
source: whereas several Vibrionales species have been found to adapt to low temperatures, such as Vibrio cholerae (Townsley et al., 2016), which was enriched under our cold conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and experimental data.

claim: Pathways related to metabolism were depleted during cold exposure in both the microbiome and host transcriptomic response.
source: Notably, our analysis revealed that pathways related to metabolism were depleted during cold exposure, in both the microbiome and host transcriptomic response (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: KEGG orthologs related to cell communication, membrane transport and structure, signaling and cell motility were enriched during cold exposure.
source: whereas KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes) orthologs related to cell communication, membrane transport and structure, signaling and cell motility were enriched, indicating a potential overall stress response (Nachin et al., 2005; Tsimring et al., 1995) (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 3 and citations to prior research.

claim: Changes in membrane transport, signal-transduction genes, tRNA diversity, and carbon metabolism have been associated with ecological fitness traits that assist in microbial survival strategies during cold adaptation in some Alteromonadales species.
source: Interestingly, such changes have also been associated with ecological fitness traits (i.e., membrane transport, signal-transduction genes, tRNA diversity, carbon metabolism) (Math et al., 2012) that assist in microbial survival strategies during cold adaptation in some Alteromonadales speciesMath et al., 2012.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The microbiome response to low temperatures is associated with the host response and is related to host thermal tolerance.
source: Motivated by the hologenome concept, we deduced that the microbiome response to low temperatures would also be associated with the host response and would be related to host thermal tolerance.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that was tested in the study.

claim: Agreement between transcriptomic and microbiome responses to cold exposure marks a host–microbiome interaction that potentially leads to higher microbiome stability and lower physiological stress in the cold-resistant fish.
source: Interestingly, we found agreement between transcriptomic and microbiome responses to cold exposure, marking a host–microbiome interaction that potentially leads to higher microbiome stability and lower physiological stress in the cold-resistant fish (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The effect on microbiome originates from differences in the genetic background, thermal tolerance and acclimation of the fish.
source: As these animals originate from different families (crosses) and not from the same population, and were kept under the same experimental conditions (same tanks) across generations, we conclude that this effect originates from differences in the genetic background, thermal tolerance and acclimation of the fish.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental design and observed results.

claim: Warmer temperatures, which are optimal for tilapias, are more permissive and can lead to greater heterogeneity and richness of microbiome composition.
source: Warmer temperatures, which are optimal for tilapias, are more permissive and can lead to greater heterogeneity and richness of microbiome composition (Erwin et al., 2012)(Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and a citation to prior research.

claim: A decrease in temperature imposes a selective pressure that reduces microbial diversity.
source: Alternatively, a decrease in temperature imposes a selective pressure that reduces microbial diversity, as we observed in both resistant and sensitive fish (Chevalier et al., 2015; Lokmer and Mathias Wegner, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior research.

claim: Host genetic background is important for microbiome composition.
source: Under warm conditions, we found compositional microbiome differences between the two host groups (Figure 2B,C,D), highlighting the importance of host genetic background for microbiome composition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The pre-exposure potential of the gut microbiome is due to host selection.
source: Nonetheless, in the transition to cold temperature, these differences in the microbiome responses in sensitive and resistant fish were manifested at the taxonomic and functional levels (Figure 2B,D,E), through enrichment of taxa with potential ecological fitness traits for cold adaptation or by affecting the cold sensitivity of the core microbial communities to temperature, and thus illustrating that the pre-exposure potential of the gut microbiome is due to host selection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cold exposure greatly affects metabolic and physiological processes in fish.
source: Cold exposure greatly affects metabolic and physiological processes in fish, which undergo several acclimation processes to maintain their fitness.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fish physiology.

claim: The transcriptomic or physiological responses to cold may include changes in enzymatic activity and efficiency, membrane permeability, and metabolic rate through mitochondrial energy production.
source: The transcriptomic or physiological responses may include changes in enzymatic activity and efficiency, membrane permeability, and metabolic rate through mitochondrial energy production (Battersby and Moyes, 1998; Itoi et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Resistant fish seemed to be under lower levels of physiological stress than sensitive fish.
source: Resistant fish seemed to be under lower levels of physiological stress than sensitive fish, and therefore had lower temperature-related metabolic demands.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the transcriptomic data.

claim: Resistant fish have lower mitochondrial gene expression than their sensitive counterparts.
source: In fact, it was previously shown that these resistant fish have lower mitochondrial gene expression than their sensitive counterparts (Nitzan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Agreement between host transcriptomic and microbiome response supports the hypothesis of host–microbe associations that potentially modulate the acclimation process.
source: Agreement between host transcriptomic and microbiome response, showing higher stability in the resistant animals compared to the sensitive ones (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplements 1–2), supports our hypothesis of host–microbe associations that potentially modulate the acclimation process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Temperature, host genetic background and tolerance to thermal stress are major determinants of community structure and dynamics.
source: Our insight into the microbial dynamics of the blue tilapia gut microbiome in response to environmental conditions shows that temperature, host genetic background and tolerance to thermal stress are major determinants of community structure and dynamics.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study findings.

claim: Microbial community diversity and richness severely decreased during cold exposure.
source: Microbial community diversity and richness severely decreased during cold exposure; but microbial response was related to host thermal tolerance, which affected microbiome stability (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 5.

claim: Host cold tolerance shapes not only gut microbiome composition but also the sensitivity of core microbial communities to temperature.
source: These results indicate that host cold tolerance shapes not only gut microbiome composition but also the sensitivity of core microbial communities to temperature, and that host cold tolerance modulates the thermal acclimation of the gut microbiome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Host cold tolerance modulates the thermal acclimation of the gut microbiome.
source: These results indicate that host cold tolerance shapes not only gut microbiome composition but also the sensitivity of core microbial communities to temperature, and that host cold tolerance modulates the thermal acclimation of the gut microbiome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The findings are consistent with the hologenome concept.
source: These finding are consistent with the hologenome concept, which proposes that associations exist between the microbes and their hosts, suggesting that together they consist a unit of natural selection.
evidence: This is a conclusion relating the findings to the theoretical framework.

claim: There are potential connections between host acclimation and its microbiome response to environmental stress.
source: Thus, taking this concept into account, we highlight potential connections between host acclimation and its microbiome response to environmental stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: The optimal temperatures for blue tilapia are 24–28°C.
source: The optimal temperatures for this species, similar to those for other tilapiine species, are 24–28°C (Trewavas, 1983)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Blue tilapia is one of the most cold-tolerant among tilapiine species.
source: but this species is one of the most cold-tolerant among this group of fish (Cnaani et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The fish's tolerance to temperatures below 16°C is transgenerational and potentially connected to maternal effects.
source: In a recent study, we found that the fish's tolerance to temperatures below 16°C is transgenerational and potentially connected to maternal effects (Nitzan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A total of 84 fish were sampled at 24°C or 12°C, originating from 3 tilapia families with high tolerance and 3 with low tolerance to cold temperatures.
source: To evaluate the responses of the fish that are resistant and sensitive to cold exposure, we challenged a total of 84 fish, sampled at 24°C or 12°C, originating from 3 tilapia families with high tolerance and 3 with low tolerance to cold temperatures (7 fish per family).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Fish were chosen originating from mothers that had the most extreme phenotypes, selected on the basis of their sibling's survival rate at low temperature.
source: For our experiments, we chose fish originating from mothers that had the most extreme phenotypes, selected on the basis of their sibling's survival rate at low temperature, as determined by previous cold-challenge trials (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1.

claim: All of the fish within each generation were kept in the same tank to eliminate confounding effects.
source: All of the fish within each generation were kept in the same tank to eliminate confounding effects.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The test groups were challenged by temperature reduction to 12°C over a period of 2 weeks.
source: The test groups, consisting of 42 fish each from resistant and sensitive families, were challenged by temperature reduction to 12°C over a period of 2 weeks and compared to a control group, consisting of 42 fish from the same families kept at 24°C.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Fish gut microbiomes were analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing.
source: At the end of the temperature-challenge trial, we analyzed the fish gut microbiomes from the test and control groups using 16S rRNA gene sequencing
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: The host's response was analyzed using liver transcriptomic analysis.
source: and we also looked at the host's response using liver transcriptomic analysis (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods shown in Figure 1.

claim: Downregulation of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) signaling and cytochrome-450-related pathways are key cell metabolism cold-induced adaptations in mice.
source: Some of the functions were actually previously reported as key cell metabolism cold-induced adaptations in mice (i.e. downregulation of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) signaling and cytochrome-450-related pathways; [Shore et al., 2013])
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: No mortality was observed during the cold challenge period.
source: Seven fish from each family were cold-challenged by gradual temperature decrease from 24°C to 12°C at a rate of 1 °C/day and then held at 12°C for 2 days, while their full-siblings were maintained at 24°C. No mortality was observed during this period.
evidence: This describes an observation from the experimental procedure.
